name: Rae Thorne
epithet: Carter of the last cart to the foot of the Steps
appearance: Twenty-seven, or near it, and strong through the shoulders in the way that comes from hauling rather than from Grace. She has a fair, open face with the wind's colour in it, grey-green eyes that stay on the road, and honey-brown hair that the hood of her cloak gives up holding, so that it falls loose past her shoulders and curls in the damp. She wears a dark hooded wool cloak pinned at the throat with a plain iron clasp over a linen shirt the colour of old cream, and a small brass bell hangs on a cord at her belt and rings whenever the cart jolts, which she never seems to hear. She drives the last cart up the Holloway to the foot of the Thousand Steps, talks to her oxen in whole sentences and to knights hardly at all, and looked at Darrow's hurt leg once, the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel.
portrait_alt: Portrait of Rae Thorne: a young woman of about twenty-seven with honey-brown hair falling loose past her shoulders, grey-green eyes and a small warm smile, in a dark hooded wool cloak pinned with a plain iron clasp over a cream linen shirt, before the stone and timber houses of a mountain village.
last_seen_doing: Sat splicing a halter on the kitchen's second bench; read the book like a load (the whole House is under it now); claimed the aye the Captain owes her.
now: In the kitchen at night, splicing a halter. The Captain owes her a plain telling of what the cold does on the stone below the House.
story_so_far: The carter who drove Darrow and Hollis the last of the road north, and who brought the House word of the Confessors' list; she let the road shut rather than leave, and when Darrow's shoulder could not shut the wicket, hers did. In the week of the Grey Cot she went down the Steps for her oxen and came up the Last Hundred at dusk with a letter in blue wax for the Captain, carried inside her shirt rather than left overnight in the cage with the grey cloak who gave it her; she won an aye off him at name-the-load and put her stake beside his in the kitchen's book. Shown the frost on Ser Benedek Orrin's mouth, she said she had had that cold in her cart, and would not say when. On the eve she stayed in the kitchen door while the House followed Wren's candle down the hall.

quote.text: The first two names on that list rode up in my cart.

known_facts.fact: She drove the last cart of the road north, a salt-cart off the Holloway, its load left at the landing to make room for two knights and a leg that was not there.
She talked to her oxen the whole of the last day and to her passengers not at all, and when Hollis started on her past the second milestone she said 'Aye' as if he had remarked on the weather.
A small brass bell hangs on a cord at her belt and rings when the cart jolts; at the foot of the Steps she rang it three times, hard, and after a while a bell answered from the cloud.
She looked at Darrow's leg once, the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel: a thing that would have to be seen to, and not by her.
known_facts.evidence: the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel: a thing that would have to be seen to, and not by her

known_facts.fact: The first of the lay brothers coming down with the litter called her Rae, as if her name were a thing you could lean on.
known_facts.evidence: as if her name were a thing you could lean on

known_facts.fact: The one thing she said to Darrow in the whole of that day, as they lifted him: 'They'll count you up. Don't help.'
known_facts.evidence: They'll count you up. Don't help.

known_facts.fact: By Wren's account she was in the taproom at the inn in Coldmere with the House's salt on her cart when the Confessors' list was read out, and heard every name.
She drove the Holloway in the dark ahead of the grey cloaks, came up the Steps before the bell, and told the winch-brothers, who told the kitchen.

Her cart stands at the winch-house at the foot of the Steps with its shafts up and two oxen in the snow; Darrow knew it from the infirmary window as the cart he had ridden the last of the Holloway in.
Wren's ledger counts one cart at the winch-house, Thorne's, and one load waiting on the cage.
At Mother Ione's council she said the list was read slow, so the room could count; and the room counted.
known_facts.evidence: So the room could count

known_facts.fact: On the stair after the council she stopped one step above Darrow, eye to eye, and asked whether he rode a grey at the ford. When he said yes and asked why, she went on up without answering; the bell at her belt rang once at the turn.
known_facts.evidence: went on up without answering

known_facts.fact: When Darrow asked to be sent down the Steps before the grey cloaks came, she said from the door that down is where they are: the first thing she had said in the council that was not an answer.
known_facts.evidence: Down's where they are

known_facts.fact: At the council, after saying down is where they are, she said she has carted men down to kneel since midsummer and has not carted one back up.
known_facts.evidence: I've not carted one back up.

known_facts.fact: From the gate wall at noon, through Sister Pell's glass, Darrow watched a grey cloak walk round her cart at the winch-house, climb onto the box and put his boots up on the board; she had not asked for the glass.

Darrow told her to go down while the rest of the grey cloaks were an hour out, ask the man off her box and be on the road to Coldmere by dark, and that once they had the cage she would be up there till the thaw; she said "Aye" to all of it. When he said he had asked fifteen times to go down those steps and she could walk down them today, she did not say aye.
known_facts.evidence: She did not say aye to that.

known_facts.fact: When the five were in at the winch-house she pinned her cloak at the throat with its iron clasp and drew up her hood; when Darrow said that had been her road, she said the first two names on that list rode up in her cart.
known_facts.evidence: The first two names on that list rode up in my cart.

known_facts.fact: Her oxen have names; asked to tell Darrow them, she said they know them.
known_facts.evidence: They know them.

known_facts.fact: Reminded that Hollis cursed everything on the road the day she drove him, she said he did the oxen before her, and something came and went at the corner of her mouth that was for the oxen.
known_facts.evidence: He did the oxen before me.

known_facts.fact: Of her oxen at the winch-house with a grey cloak on her cart: they'll stand; a mule won't stand at the winch-house, and an ox will stand all winter.
known_facts.evidence: An ox'll stand all winter.

known_facts.fact: When Darrow's knee began to shake from the standing, she sat down at one end of the gate-ward's bench, and he sat at the other before he had decided to; then she said, once, to the valley, that his leg was shaking.
known_facts.evidence: Leg was shaking

known_facts.fact: Asked on the gate wall why she had asked whether he rode a grey at the ford, she said, to the valley, that carters look at horses; Darrow saw her hands, between her knees, close on each other.
known_facts.evidence: Carters look at horses.

known_facts.fact: She left the bench on the first stroke of the hour bell, and at the turn of the walk stopped and said that the near one of her oxen is the slow one.
known_facts.evidence: The near one's the slow one

known_facts.fact: At the reading she stood at the end of the lay brothers' line in the court, as still as anything she had ever driven.
known_facts.evidence: as still as anything she had ever driven

known_facts.fact: When a third grey cloak held the wicket open and it threw Darrow off, her shoulder went in under the gate-ward's, set as she would set it to a cart gone into a rut, and the wicket shut on the man's arm.
known_facts.evidence: set as she would set it to a cart gone into a rut

known_facts.fact: When Darrow had given his name at the bars she was rubbing the shoulder she had put to the wicket and watching him the way she had watched the valley from the wall.
known_facts.evidence: rubbing the shoulder she had put to the wicket

known_facts.fact: She took the Steps down without counting, like a road, and never looked back at the gate; at the winch-house she went to the near ox's head and stood there until the grey cloak got off her box.
known_facts.evidence: She went to the near ox's head and stood there

known_facts.fact: Her oxen are stabled in the winch-house byre with a grey cloak's stool in the door; the Confessors' cart has flour out of Coldmere for six men to the thaw and past it, and they bake it on the House's wood.
known_facts.evidence: for six men to the thaw and past it

known_facts.fact: The near ox is Hob: she said his name once, unasked, and nobody remarked on it.
known_facts.evidence: Hob won't eat with him there.

known_facts.fact: She brought up a letter in blue wax for the Captain of the Ninth at the House of Menders, and when he asked who gave it her she said only that it came up with her.
known_facts.evidence: It came up with me.

known_facts.fact: She called him Darrow, not Ser, not Captain: she does not drive for the Ninth, she drives for the House.
known_facts.evidence: I don't drive for the Ninth.

known_facts.fact: Her grandmother was Thornwild-born and came over the Wend behind a drover, long before the ford; Coldmere called the family the Thornwild woman's, and it wore down to Thorne, and they kept it.
known_facts.evidence: Coldmere called us the Thornwild woman's, and it wore down to Thorne.

known_facts.fact: When she told him her grandmother was Thornwild-born, she watched him take it.
known_facts.evidence: She watched him take that.

known_facts.fact: She does not count the Steps: counting is for Wren and for men with lists, and a road you count gets longer under you.
known_facts.evidence: Rae Thorne did not count the Steps at all.

known_facts.fact: At the winch-house she stood at Hob's head with her hand on his neck until the grey cloak got off her box with a little bow, and she let him think it was manners.
known_facts.evidence: she let him think it was manners

known_facts.fact: Her other ox is Dun.
known_facts.evidence: put his nose in her armpit

known_facts.fact: She read the Confessors' cart by what it ate: flour with the Coldmere mill's mark, for six men to the thaw and past it, and nobody brings that for a paper they mean to read at a gate and take home.
known_facts.evidence: Nobody brings flour past the thaw for a paper they mean to read at a gate and take home.

known_facts.fact: The grey cloak at the winch-house gave her the letter, saying the Captain of the Ninth twice with a smile, the way you say the name of a horse you have already bought.
known_facts.evidence: the way you say the name of a horse you have already bought

known_facts.fact: Rather than leave the letter a night at the bottom of the cage with him sitting over it, she put it inside her shirt and carried it up herself.
known_facts.evidence: She took it out of his hand and put it inside her shirt, wax inward.

known_facts.fact: Before she started up she told Hob she would tell Darrow he would not eat.
known_facts.evidence: I'll tell Darrow you wouldn't.

known_facts.fact: She judged the Captain's bet on NOBODY a light load for a long road.
known_facts.evidence: Light load," she said, "for a long road.

known_facts.fact: She put her own stake beside his: if a cot goes grey before the thaw, she carries the kitchen a load up the Steps on her back, not the cage, whatever it wants.
known_facts.evidence: I carry this kitchen a load up the Steps. On my back, not the cage.

known_facts.fact: She will come up the Steps again when she owes.
known_facts.evidence: And come up when I'm owing.

known_facts.fact: She holds that a carter says who a load is for, not whose hand it came out of, and the man it is for least of all.
known_facts.evidence: A carter says who a load's for. Not whose hand it came out of.

known_facts.fact: She told Darrow to read the letter, then ask her again if he still wanted to.
known_facts.evidence: Read it. Then ask me again, if you still want to.

known_facts.fact: Carters play name-the-load at every winch on the Holloway: you name a load before it is up, by how it hangs.
known_facts.evidence: Carters play it at every winch on the Holloway.

known_facts.fact: She read the first load as wet linen: salt sits like a stone, that was sitting like a drunk.
known_facts.evidence: Salt sits like a stone. That's sitting like a drunk.

known_facts.fact: She will claim the aye he owes her some day, and will know what for when she asks.
known_facts.evidence: I'll know when I ask.

known_facts.fact: Shown the frost on the lad's mouth, she said she has had that cold in her cart.
known_facts.evidence: I've had that cold in my cart

known_facts.fact: Asked when, she said only Aye.
known_facts.evidence: which was no answer to anything

known_facts.fact: She did not ask him about the letter.
known_facts.evidence: She did not ask about the letter.

known_facts.fact: She told the Captain the grey cloak at the winch-house gave her the letter, and said the Captain of the Ninth twice, smiling the second time.
known_facts.evidence: The grey cloak at the winch-house

known_facts.fact: She would not leave the letter overnight in the cage with that man sitting over it, so she carried it up herself.
known_facts.evidence: A night's a long time for a letter to lie at the bottom of a cage

known_facts.fact: She does not count the Steps; Wren does.
known_facts.evidence: I don't count them. Wren does.

known_facts.fact: Asked again about the cold in her cart, she said he gets one question a night and has had it.
known_facts.evidence: You get one a night

known_facts.fact: She alone stayed in the kitchen door and watched the flame lie down from there, the way you watch weather you have already been out in.
known_facts.evidence: the way you watch weather you have already been out in

known_facts.fact: She read the kitchen's book like a load and said the whole House is under it now.
known_facts.evidence: Heavy book," she said. "Whole House is under it now.

known_facts.fact: She claimed her aye: when the Captain has been down the stair he is to tell her what the cold does on the stone, plain, not how he would tell the House.
known_facts.evidence: I'll have my aye.

relationships.label: the knight she drove to the foot of the Steps
relationships.note: She looked at his leg once the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel, rang for the litter, and said one thing to him all day; seven weeks after the Binding he knew her cart from the infirmary window and had not forgotten it. When the grey cloaks came in, he told her from the gate wall to go while the road was open, and she let it shut. At the wicket her shoulder went in where his had given, and she watched him give his name at the bars.

relationships.label: the old knight who cursed her from her own cart
relationships.note: When he started on her past the second milestone she said 'Aye' as if he had remarked on the weather, and the cart went on.

relationships.label: the runner who carried her news into the hall
relationships.note: Wren told the infirmary hall that Rae had heard the list read at Coldmere, driven through the dark ahead of the grey cloaks and climbed the Steps before the bell.

deeper: She says a thing once, and "Aye" does the work of a paragraph.
